Tesla Model X on Autopilot/FSD hit a pole and flipped, killing passenger

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger.
  • Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and claims it has the car’s event data recorder and video.
  • In a recent development, at 11:43 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model X veered off Golden Gate Parkway in Naples, Florida, hit a traffic signal pole and overturned in September, killing a 50-year-old woman riding as a passenger. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators states Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged.

Tesla flagged this crash itself, through its telematics, and claims it has the car’s event data recorder and video. The public was told a car “veered off the road.” It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

In a recent development, at 11:43 p.m. on Wednesday, September 30, 2026, a 2025 Tesla Model X was heading east on Golden Gate Parkway in Collier County, approaching the Estuary Boulevard intersection, according to a Florida Highway Patrol press release.

The SUV left the road, hit a traffic signal pole on the corner of the intersection, and rolled over. Its passenger, a 50-year-old woman from Fort Myers, was pronounced dead at the scene. The 48-year-old driver, also from Fort Myers, went to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

In a recent development, FHP said the crash remains under investigation. It hasn’t released the woman’s name, a cause, or anything about speed or impairment. And nothing about a driver-assist system.

In a recent development, under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

According to recent reports, it identifies a 2025 Model X and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged,” meaning Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 39 mph, a collision with a pole or tree, airbag deployment, and damage to the front and the top of the car, which fits FHP’s account of the rollover.

According to recent reports, this record is unusually complete on what Tesla has. It checks the event data recorder, telematics, video, and “other.” And it says Tesla learned of the crash through its own telematics, not just from the media.

Then it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 03:41 UTC on October 1, which is 11:41 p.m. in Florida on September 30, two minutes off FHP’s 11:43 p.m. The city, the 2025 Model X, the pole, and the fatal outcome all line up. Because the UTC timestamp crosses midnight, Tesla’s record lists the crash in October, so anyone checking Tesla’s data against September crashes would miss it. It’s the same crash.

Most of the crashes we’ve matched leave real gaps in what Tesla holds. Not this one. Tesla has the video, the EDR, and the telematics, and it knew about the crash on its own.

Industry observers note that so Tesla can see what the car did on the approach to that intersection. It knows whether the system steered the SUV off the road or the driver did, whether the car warned him, and how fast it was going when it hit the pole. It filed all of that under a redaction.

Autopilot/FSD might not have caused the crash, but it was active within 30 seconds of the crash, so it’s key to understand what happened. Was the driver distracted? Did Autopilot/FSD make a run move?

There’s also a living witness here. The driver survived with non-life-threatening injuries, which means FHP can ask him whether he had Autopilot or FSD on and what the car was doing. We don’t know if anyone has. Troopers may not even know Tesla verified the system was engaged.

This is the second fatal Tesla driver-assist crash in Naples in this NHTSA release. In May, a Model 3 with the system engaged at 71 mph hit an overturned box truck on I-75 at Pine Ridge Road, killing three people. FHP investigated both, and neither crash was ever publicly tied to Autopilot or FSD.

The same release set a new record: 264 Tesla driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236.

Industry observers note that this is the cleanest example yet of how much Tesla knows and how little it shares. It detected the crash on its own. It has the video. It has the EDR. A woman riding as a passenger died in a Model X that, according to Tesla, had its driver-assist engaged. And the public account is one sentence: the car veered off the road.

In a recent development, tesla certainly benefits by keeping the information hidden. Most are willing to look past these things and not be suspicious, but ultimately the question is why hide. something if you dont have something to hide.

According to recent reports, we’re not saying the system caused this crash. We don’t know, and that’s the point. Tesla does know, and it decided the account of what its car did in a fatal crash is a trade secret.

In a recent development, if FSD or Autopilot did nothing wrong here, Tesla has the footage to prove it. It was happy to share data in the Katy crash when it helped its case. When Tesla keeps the video sealed, people are going to assume the worst, and Tesla only has itself to blame.

Sources indicate that we’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol whether its investigators knew the system was engaged and whether they got Tesla’s video and raw data, or only Tesla’s interpretation of them. Same questions we asked about Vineland. How many more fatal crashes will troopers close without knowing what Tesla knows?

Sources indicate that ripple's U.S. dollar stablecoin Ripple USD (RLUSD) has overtaken Gram (GRAM), the token previously known as Toncoin, in the CoinMarketCap ranking of cryptocurrencies by market capitalization.

According to CoinMarketCap data, RLUSD had a market capitalization of $2.82 billion on Tuesday and ranked No. 26, and Gram dropped to No. 27 with a market capitalization of $2.79 billion.

Gram fell below $1 and was trading at around $0.97 on Tuesday, down about 6% over the past seven days, according to CoinMarketCap. The 24-hour trading volume of Gram stood at around $47 million, and RLUSD had about $368 million in trading volume over the same period.

World Liberty Financial USD (USD1) also had a market capitalization of $2.82 billion on Tuesday and was one spot higher, at No. 25. Among stablecoins, Tether (USDT) and USDC still lead the list with $174.64 billion and $69.22 billion, respectively.

In late July, the market value of RLUSD was about $1.5 billion, according to RWA.xyz data. On Aug. 25, Ripple noted that RLUSD had crossed $2 billion in market capitalization, with close to $1 billion of the supply issued on the XRP Ledger. By mid-September, RLUSD supply stood at $2.44 billion.

In late October, the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave Ripple approval for Ripple National Trust Bank. A day later, on Oct. 27, Moody's Ratings assigned RLUSD an A2 long-term deposit rating and a P-1 short-term deposit rating. RLUSD is issued by Ripple subsidiary Standard Custody & Trust Company. Also in late October, RLUSD became available on Coinbase and Robinhood.

Industry observers note that the Open Network renamed its token from Toncoin to Gram in June 2026. On July 21, Telegram founder Pavel Durov announced a native non-custodial Gram wallet for every Telegram app. "This summer will see the largest rollout of a non-custodial crypto wallet in human history. Instant zero-fee crypto transactions for over a billion users are about to become reality," Durov wrote.

This week, Telegram published the terms of service for Gram Wallet. According to the terms, the wallet is operated by RAZOR UNIVERSAL CORP., a Panamanian tech giant, and Telegram provides the apps through which owners access it. "Telegram does not operate Gram Wallet, does not hold your keys or assets, and is not a party to these Terms," the document notes.

The terms also say that "neither we nor Telegram can freeze, seize, move, recover or reverse your assets." At the same time, according to the terms, "anyone who visits your Telegram profile may be able to see your associated Gram Wallet address," as well as the total balance of the wallet. Access to the wallet "may be restricted or unavailable in certain regions or to certain customers," the document says.

In a recent development, onchain Lens reported over $600,000 lost from one user’s Trezor and Exodus wallets on the 23rd of November. The Trezor wallet theft report raised a harder question: how did transfers use the victim’s signing authority without their claimed approval?

Sources indicate that the blockchain investigator listed approximately $580,000 in Tether [USDT] losses on TRON and $23,400 in USD Coin [USDC] on Solana. Another $9,500 reportedly disappeared from an Exodus wallet on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max.

Reportedly, the victim generated the recovery phrase on Trezor and kept it on paper and refused to allow anyone physical access to the device.

A 49,999 USDT transfer on the 21st of November used the TRON account’s default owner permission. It was a direct transfer, with no transfer from operation drawing on an existing token allowance.

It has been revealed that on Solana [SOL], the examined instruction identified the victim’s wallet as the transfer authority, signer, and fee payer. Notably, no separate delegate appeared.

These transfers used the wallet’s signing authority. However, it is unclear how someone gained that access.

It has been revealed that A valid signature authorizes a transaction on the network. So, it cannot establish whether the owner knowingly approved it. The Trezor accounts on both chains shared one recovery phrase, making that backup a possible link between the losses.

In an X reply, Trezor said similar cases usually involved “a compromised wallet backup.”.

It’s hard to say what happened here without more details.

It has been revealed that the company asked the affected user to contact official support. Its reply offered a possible explanation, without establishing this incident’s cause.

Industry observers note that trezor indicates its Bluetooth chip cannot access private keys. On the other hand, Exodus says its Trezor integration also leaves those keys inside the hardware. Whether the user enabled that integration remains unclear.

Apple’s 9th of November enhancement patched Bluetooth issues, but Onchain Lens found no evidence linking those vulnerabilities to these transfers.

Earlier incidents show why identifying the route matters.

It has been revealed that as AMBCrypto reported, Trezor confirmed implants in three CryptoBilis-sold Safe 5 devices on the 12th of November. Those implants captured recovery words from device screens.

Separately, Confiant’s MoldyRoost research documented another route; malicious ads delivering exploits to vulnerable iPhones. Furthermore, Chainalysis counted roughly 158,000 personal-wallet compromise incidents affecting 80,000 victims in 2025.

For this user, the unanswered question is specific: how did someone obtain signing access across the affected wallets?

#122559. Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1743 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Motorcycles are notoriously dangerous. Could electric motorcycles actually change that?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety.
  • But that simple statement also hides something notable.
  • Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there’s no particularly comfortable way to talk about motorcycle safety. Motorcycles are dangerous. All the statistics point to the fact that per mile, motorcycles are significantly more dangerous. And as someone who promotes them as a better alternative to large cars and trucks for many trips, it’s an uncomfortable reality that must be grappled with.

But that simple statement also hides something notable. Not all motorcycles, riders, or riding behaviors carry the same risk. And as a new generation of smaller electric motorcycles begins to emerge, I think there’s an interesting question worth asking: Could electric motorcycles inadvertently make motorcycling safer?

Not because electricity is somehow safer than gasoline. It isn’t. Rather, because electrification may fundamentally change the type of motorcycle that hits the road.

In 2024, 6,228 motorcyclists were killed in the US, accounting for 16% of all traffic fatalities, according to the NHTSA.

In a recent development, obviously, motorcycles have a fundamental disadvantage here. You don’t have a steel cage around you. There aren’t crumple zones separating your body from an oncoming SUV. There’s no seatbelt holding you in place or curtain airbag waiting to catch your head.

But there’s another component to motorcycle fatalities that is harder to ignore: rider behavior.

Around 35% of motorcyclist deaths in 2024 occurred in single-vehicle crashes, according to the IIHS. In other words, more than one-third of those deaths didn’t involve a rider being hit by another vehicle. At that point, whether or not a crash occurred was essentially in the hands of the rider.

Alcohol is another major factor. Among riders killed in single-vehicle crashes, the NHTSA reports that 40% were alcohol-impaired.

Then there are the bikes themselves.

Supersport motorcycles stand out for all the wrong reasons. Of the riders killed on supersports in 2024, 59% were under 30. Compare that to cruiser and standard motorcycles, where just 19% of killed riders were under 30, or touring motorcycles at only 7%.

In a recent development, that’s not proof that powerful motorcycles are causing those deaths, of course. There are all sorts of confounding factors, including the type of person attracted to different motorcycles and how those motorcycles tend to be ridden.

But it’s hard to ignore the broader picture.

To put it more plainly, a huge portion of motorcycle deaths are caused by riders simply going too fast, doing something wrong (like drinking or taking turns too aggressively), or because they couldn’t handle the power of an insanely high-performance crotch rocket. So while figures such as “motorcycles are 27x more deadly than cars” might be true in a broad sense, that doesn’t mean you have a 27x higher chance of death – especially not if you aren’t a 25-year-old hooligan on a second-hand liter bike.

One of the strange things about motorcycling is just how cheaply you can buy extraordinary performance.

According to recent reports, someone with relatively little riding experience can buy a used supersport capable of acceleration that would have required an exotic supercar not long ago. The motorcycle may weigh around 400 lb, produce well over 100 horsepower, and be capable of speeds approaching three times a typical US highway speed limit.

And unlike cars, there isn’t much protecting you when that performance gets away from you.

That’s why I find the current evolution of electric motorcycles so interesting.

Sources indicate that for years, electric motorcycle companies largely chased gasoline motorcycles up the performance ladder. We got incredibly fast and powerful machines from companies like Energica and LiveWire.

Those bikes proved electric motorcycles could be fast.

But I’m increasingly interested in the opposite end of the spectrum.

Look at motorcycles such as LiveWire’s upcoming S4 Honcho.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t an electric superbike designed around insane acceleration or a 150 mph (240 km/h) top speed. It’s a smaller motorcycle intended to offer approachable performance at a more accessible price.

It adds to a growing market already populated by highly acclaimed modest-sized electric motorcycles like those from Ryvid, Land, and Maeving.

And we’re seeing more machines begin to occupy this previously neglected territory between an e-bike and a full-size motorcycle.

That could make a huge difference when it comes to overall safety, as crotch rockets get replaced by sensible electric motorbikes.

Sources indicate that battery technology actually creates an interesting incentive here. Making an electric motorcycle ridiculously powerful is easy. Giving it enough battery to sustain high speeds for long distances without becoming extremely heavy and expensive is much, much harder.

So the economics and physics of batteries naturally make smaller urban and suburban motorcycles fairly compelling right now.

Instead of asking how to build another 150 mph (240 km/h) electric motorcycle, manufacturers can build a lighter machine that goes 60 or 70 mph (95-120 km/h), has enough range for everyday riding, and costs considerably less.

Ironically, one of the limitations most commonly leveled against electric motorcycles could turn out to have a safety upside.

This is where I think things get even more interesting.

According to recent reports, for decades, the stereotypical progression into motorcycling might have involved learning on a dirt bike or small displacement motorcycle, then moving fairly promptly into larger machines. Often though, new riders simply took a licensing course and then bought their first 600cc sport bike to learn to ride.

But now we’re raising an entirely newly introduced generation on electric two-wheelers.

Kids and teenagers are increasingly growing up riding e-bikes and small electric motos. Eventually, many of them are going to want something faster than a 20 or 28 mph e-bike.

A 50 mph (80 km/h) electric motorcycle is a pretty logical next step for the e-moto kids of today. Eventually, perhaps that rider graduates to something capable of 70 or 80 mph (120-130 km/h) and comfortable highway travel.

That’s a much more gradual performance curve than jumping from essentially no powered two-wheeler experience to a screaming 600cc supersport.

According to recent reports, there’s another advantage too: electric motorcycles are mechanically easier to operate. There’s generally no clutch, no gearbox, and no concern about stalling. Twist the throttle and go.

That doesn’t necessarily make them safer – instant electric torque can certainly get an inexperienced rider into trouble – but it does remove several tasks from the mental workload of learning to ride.

It has been revealed that the rider can spend more attention on braking, cornering, traffic, positioning, and the thousand other things that actually keep you alive on a motorcycle. The reduction in cognitive load can mean more focus on control, if it’s used that way.

To be clear, I’m not arguing that electric motorcycles are inherently safe.

It has been revealed that they’re still motorcycles and they still lack cages. Well, most of them.

If an inattentive driver turns left in front of you, the chemistry powering your rear wheel isn’t going to make much difference.

In a recent development, and electric motorcycles can be outrageously powerful. In fact, the instantaneous torque of an electric motor can make poor throttle calibration especially unforgiving for inexperienced riders.

There also simply isn’t enough data yet to demonstrate that electric motorcycles have meaningfully lower fatality rates than comparable gasoline motorcycles.

But that’s not really my argument.

In a recent development, my argument is that electrification may change what we consider a normal beginner motorcycle. And that could be much more notable, helping to significantly reduce accidents and deaths.

I’m never going to pretend motorcycles can become as safe as cars. The physics simply don’t work that way.

But the broad statistic of “motorcycles are dangerous” encompasses an enormous spectrum of machines and riders.

A sober, trained commuter wearing proper protective gear and riding a modestly powered motorcycle to work is doing something fundamentally different from an inexperienced 21-year-old seeing how fast his supersport can take an empty freeway ramp at 2 a.m.

Yet both contribute to the same broad motorcycle fatality statistics.

Recent findings suggest that what excites me about this emerging generation of electric motorcycles isn’t that swapping gasoline for batteries magically fixes motorcycle safety. It obviously doesn’t.

I bought a motorcycle around age 60 after considering the risk factors I could control:.

Sources indicate that I took a MSF basic riding course before buying the motorcycle. Best investment in the whole saga.

Industry observers note that I never rode impaired. That was easy.

I always rode with full protection. That was doable but inconvenient and seriously uncomfortable in hot weather.

I never rode in rainy weather or at night. Again possible but limited my use of the motorcycle for commuting. Eventually my schedule changed to evening and stopped my motorcycle commuting altogether.

In a recent development, after a few close calls I started avoiding roads with more than one lane in each direction. That added quite a bit to my commute time.

Recent findings suggest that I never rode when I was in a hurry. That meant more days I didn't use the motorcycle for commuting.

None of these precautions have anything to do with electric drive. After I sold my gas motorcycle I test rode an electric motorcycle and loved it. However I didn't buy it because it didn't reduce any of the risks and I wouldn't ride it more than the gas bike.

It’s that electrification could help create a newly introduced category of desirable, affordable motorcycles that don’t need 120 horsepower and a 160 mph top speed to be cool.

If younger riders grow up progressing from e-bikes to small e-motos and then to highway-capable electric motorcycles, perhaps we’ll wind up with a generation that sees a lightweight 60 or 70 mph motorcycle as a perfectly legitimate machine rather than merely a stepping stone to something ridiculously powerful.

Maybe electrification’s biggest contribution to motorcycle safety won’t be traction control, ABS, or sophisticated electronics.

Maybe it’ll simply make sensible motorcycles fun and cool again.

Are Ripple’s XRP, Cardano (ADA), and Polygon (POL) losing their appeal among crypto investors in 2026? Ben Simpson, founder of crypto investment platform Collective Shift, has named all three among six altcoins he says he wouldn’t touch with a 10-foot pole, citing concerns ranging from weak network activity and questionable valuations to intensifying competition. His blunt assessment raises fresh questions about which altcoins have the strongest fundamentals to survive the increasingly competitive crypto market.

In his post on X, Simpson acknowledged XRP’s role in enabling near-instant, inexpensive payments on the XRP Ledger but argued that the token lacks a compelling mechanism for capturing the value generated by Ripple’s business growth.

XRP enables fast, low-cost payments on the XRP Ledger.My glitch with XRP is it's "value capture".When a business grows, I want to see how that success benefits the token I'm holding. In this case, there is none. Ripple can grow its revenue, but holders don't receive those….

His main concern is that Ripple’s commercial success does not necessarily translate into direct financial benefits for XRP holders. Even as the San Francisco-headquartered tech giant expands its revenue and boosts its payment operations, investors do not receive a share of those profits.

In a recent development, he also pointed out that Ripple does not use its business earnings to buy back XRP, a mechanism that could potentially create additional demand for the token. For Simpson, the absence of both profit-sharing and a buyback program makes it difficult to establish a direct link between Ripple’s growing business and XRP’s price in the long term.

He considers these shortcomings significant enough to keep XRP off his investment list, despite the network’s payment capabilities.

Simpson also expressed reservations about Cardano, arguing that its adoption level does not justify its market valuation. Although ADA powers a blockchain designed to support smart contracts and decentralized applications, he believes the network is generating relatively little economic activity compared with its overall market size.

To support his argument, Simpson pointed to Cardano’s fee generation, claiming that the network collected just $140,000 in transaction fees over a 30-day period despite ADA carrying a market capitalization of approximately $7.5 billion.

Sources indicate that for him, the disparity raises questions about whether Cardano is attracting enough users and developers to sustain its valuation. He believes a blockchain with such a substantial market capitalization should demonstrate considerably stronger usage and demand for its services.

According to recent reports, ultimately, Simpson’s concern is that Cardano needs to translate its technological ambitions and established ecosystem into greater real-world activity. Without a meaningful increase in network usage, he appears unconvinced that ADA offers an attractive investment proposition.

In a recent development, polygon also made the list, with concerns centered on the growing competition in Ethereum’s scaling ecosystem. Although POL supports a network designed to make transactions faster and cheaper, the increasing number of competing blockchain solutions has made it harder for Polygon to maintain a distinctive advantage.

Simpson’s concern is that newer networks are offering similar benefits, including lower transaction costs and faster processing speeds, leaving Polygon with fewer obvious ways to differentiate itself.

With several projects competing for developers, people, and blockchain activity, POL faces the challenge of proving why it deserves a place ahead of its rivals.

In a recent development, beyond XRP, Cardano, and Polygon, three other cryptocurrencies also fell short of Ben Simpson’s investment criteria: Sui (SUI), Ronin (RON), and Dogwifhat (WIF). Unlike his concerns about the first three crypto projects, his reservations about these tokens stem largely from changing investment convictions, disappointing adoption, and excessive reliance on market hype.

According to recent reports, sui was among the projects Simpson previously held before changing his investment outlook. The high-speed blockchain is designed to support decentralized applications and transactions, but he eventually dumped his SUI holdings at a loss of between 20% and 30% after his investment thesis changed. He did not elaborate on the specific developments that prompted his decision.

According to recent reports, ronin was another project he abandoned after its growth failed to match his expectations. Initially attracted by the potential of blockchain gaming, the pundit bought into the network, which uses RON for transaction fees and staking. However, the anticipated expansion in gaming adoption did not materialize as he had hoped, prompting him to exit the position relatively swiftly. He argued that strong sector potential means little without meaningful retail participation.

WIF, meanwhile, represented a different kind of investment mistake. Simpson admitted that his decision to buy the Solana-based meme coin was driven largely by hype rather than underlying fundamentals. After his investment thesis changed, he sold his holdings to limit further losses.

His experience with WIF appears to have reinforced his preference for cryptocurrencies backed by stronger fundamentals rather than speculative excitement.

To back the data, Grayscale revealed charts comparing Bitcoin's performance across historical bear markets that ended in June 2011, December 2013, December 2017, November 2021, and the ongoing October 2025 cycle.

While the 2011, 2017 and 2021 bear cycles suffered massive losses, especially during the former when its indexed performance fell below 10, the current 2025 bear market broke historical pattern by enduring a longer period yet a comparatively modest decline in Bitcoin’s price.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although the CLARTIY Act failed to pass the Senate this year, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is working hard to develop upcoming crypto market advisories.
  • According to recent reports, on the 23rd of November, the agency issued a newly introduced advisory allowing certain crypto assets to be counted towards the financial resource requirements of regulated derivatives trading and clearing platforms.
  • So now, Swap Execution Facilities (SEFs), Designated Contract Markets (DCMs), and Derivatives Clearing Organizations (DCOs) can use these digital assets to confirm that they have sufficient financial resources to cover at least 12 months of operating expenses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although the CLARTIY Act failed to pass the Senate this year, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is working hard to develop upcoming crypto market advisories.

According to recent reports, on the 23rd of November, the agency issued a newly introduced advisory allowing certain crypto assets to be counted towards the financial resource requirements of regulated derivatives trading and clearing platforms. This includes Bitcoin [BTC], Ethereum [ETH], and payment stablecoins.

So now, Swap Execution Facilities (SEFs), Designated Contract Markets (DCMs), and Derivatives Clearing Organizations (DCOs) can use these digital assets to confirm that they have sufficient financial resources to cover at least 12 months of operating expenses.

These requirements are designed to ensure that such platforms have enough funds to continue operating and meet their financial obligations, even during times of financial stress.

However, the approval comes with an crucial limitation. While eligible crypto assets can contribute towards the 12-month financial resources requirement, they cannot be counted towards the separate liquidity requirement. This is because, under Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP), cryptocurrencies are not classified as cash or highly liquid securities.

In simple terms, holding Bitcoin or Ethereum may help a platform prove its financial strength, but it cannot replace the cash or highly liquid assets it needs to meet immediate payment obligations.

The advisory also requires appropriate haircuts. In other words, the platforms must discount the value of crypto assets when calculating how much they can count towards their financial resources. This would be done to account for the price volatility and risks associated with digital assets.

Expressing their opinion on the matter, CFTC’s Chairman Mike Selig noted,.

Pleased to see @CFTC staff continue to provide crucial clarity around crypto assets in US derivatives markets through today’s staff advisory.

Recent findings suggest that on the same day, though, the CFTC also introduced a new reporting framework for certain fully collateralized event contracts. This was done to replace the reliance on temporary regulatory exemptions and no-action letters that have been in place since 2017.

In other words, the move aims to make reporting requirements for event contracts, including prediction-market products, clearer and more consistent.

Remarking on this, Selig noted,.

Yet, despite all the efforts, Senator Adam Schiff criticized the Trump-appointed CFTC Chairman over his handling of the legal battle surrounding prediction markets. Schiff claims that the chairman had previously told the Senate during his confirmation process that he would allow courts to decide whether prediction markets fall under gambling laws.

However, according to Schiff, the chairman has since acted against that commitment. Schiff believes that Selig has allegedly disregarded court orders and intervened in ongoing litigation in ways that favor the prediction-market industry.

His criticism suggests that the CFTC leadership is taking an active role in protecting prediction-market platforms rather than maintaining regulatory neutrality.

All of this coincided with the agency’s looks to use its existing authority to introduce two initiatives: Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM).

Industry observers note that not all commutes are created equal, and tackling a hard commute takes a lot more than a motor and a set of wheels. Ausom knows this better than most, with six highly capable, long-range electric scooters designed to handle your toughest trips. And this Black Friday, you can get the right tool for the job at the lowest prices of the year.

Industry observers note that there’s a difference between owning an electric scooter you haul out the farmer’s market every few months and actually riding one every day. If you’re just covering the occasional trip around the neighborhood, almost anything with two wheels and a battery will probably do. But if you’re depending on your scooter to handle a hard commute climbing hills, navigating broken pavement, and covering serious distances ever day, the right equipment matters – and Ausom has the right equipment for just about any ride.

From November 16-December 1, Ausom’s has the right equipment making that decision a little easier this Black Friday, with its entire electric scooter lineup hitting its lowest prices of 2026 and additional savings available exclusively to Electrek readers when they use the code ElectrekFB at checkout.

Recent findings suggest that before diving into the individual e-scooter breakdowns, let’s first take a look at the flash sale deals available throughout the event. These limited-stock offers will run from 9 p.m. to 10 p.m. EST and cannot be combined with the exclusive discount code or any free gifts.

With six different models on offer this shopping season, Ausom has the right ride for just about every kind of rider, from everyday campus commuters looking for dependable transportation between bells to high-strung adrenaline junkies ready to push the limits of tiny, two-wheeled performance. Here’s the rundown:.

Industry observers note that built for real-world roads, the Gosoul 2 offers smooth, quiet, and confident travel across city streets, wet roads, and light gravel with puncture-resistant 10×2.5″ tubeless tires that reduce the risk of flats, enhance grip, and reduce maintenance needs for everyday dependability. E-ABS brakes cut motor power for faster responses and shorter stopping distances with superior control, while the powerful, 1100W motor, 70 km (~44 miles) of range, and ability to haul riders up 20% grade hills make the Gosoul 2 a great choice for any tech-savvy commuter.

Regularly priced at $729, the Gosoul 2 is on sale this month for just $569, and $549 for Electrek readers.

It has been revealed that for riders who want something more than basic transportation, the L2 Max Dual Motor brings serious performance to city streets, hills and gravel rides. Its dual 1,000W brushless motors deliver up to 2,688W of peak power, giving riders the extra muscle to accelerate confidently, climb steep neighborhood hills and keep moving when the pavement ends. A nearly 1 kWh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of range, making longer commutes and multiple stops around town easier to manage between charges. The 10×3″ puncture-resistant tubeless tires help maintain traction while reducing the risk of flats, and an adjustable dual swingarm suspension smooths out potholes, cracked pavement and rough gravel. With a top speed of 38 mph and the ability to tackle grades up to 34%, the L2 Max has plenty of performance in reserve for hard commutes and demanding rides, while its front and rear disc brakes with E-ABS help bring that power under control when traffic (or wildlife) demands a quick stop.

Regularly priced at $1,049, the L2 Max Dual Motor is on sale this month for $809, and $799 for Electrek readers.

Built for riders who refuse to choose between range and performance, the DT2 Pro packs dual 1,100W motors producing more than 2,900W of peak power. That’s enough muscle to tackle steep hills and grades of up to 36%, even when the route gets challenging, while its nearly 40 mph top speed gives riders plenty of acceleration for open stretches. The DT2’s 1.22 kWh battery delivers up to 115 km (~71 miles) of claimed range, making it a strong option for longer commutes or riders who want to cover several trips without stopping to recharge. Its 10×3″ puncture-resistant tires provide a wider contact patch for added traction, while an adjustable suspension front and rear helps absorb bumps, cracks, and rough patches to keep the rider stable and comfortable across changing terrain.

Regularly priced at $1,349, the DT2 Pro is on sale this month for $1,069, and $1,059 for Electrek readers.

Industry observers note that taking the Gosoul 2 to the next level, the Gosoul 2 Pro Dual Motor packs a pair of 1,400W motors for a 36 mph top speed and the ability to tackle grades of up to 33%. An 864 Wh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of range, while the Ausom ShocFree dual swingarm suspension and 10×2.75″ tubeless tires help keep things smooth and stable on all kinds of roads and paths.

Regularly priced at $999, the Gosoul 2 Pro Dual Motor is on sale for $829, and $799 for Electrek readers.

The K20 Pro Dual Motor packs plenty of performance into a more approachable package, with dual 1,400W motors delivering 2,800W of peak power – more than enough to give riders the go-power they need to carve up modern day traffic and tackle grades of up to 33%, while its 36 mph top speed leaves plenty of headroom for open stretches. Its 864 Wh battery provides up to 90 km (~56 miles) of claimed range, making it a practical option for hard commutes or a full day of riding around town. ShocFree suspension and 10×2.75″ tubeless tires help smooth out potholes, uneven pavement and light off-road sections, while front and rear disc brakes with E-ABS provide maximum control during emergency stops.

Regularly priced at $879, the K20 Pro Dual Motor is on sale for just $689, and Electrek readers can do even better at $679.

In a recent development, just like it says on the tin, the F1 Max offers maximum performance inspired by the pinnacle of motorsport. Built for riders who want their electric scooter to be considerably more than a commuter, this one delivers up to 3,840W of peak power, pushing the F1 Max to speeds of up to 45 mph and allowing it to tackle grades as steep as 38%. A 1.25 kWh battery pack gives riders 100 km (~62 miles) of range, while an adjustable dual-swingarm suspension and 10×3″ tubeless tires give the scooter the hardware to handle everything from broken city pavement and gravel to light off-road trails. Hydraulic disc brakes with E-ABS help bring all that performance back under control, while a 330 lb. maximum load and wide deck make the F1 Max a substantial machine for bigger, bolder riders ready for longer trips into the wilderness and anyone looking for a little LOT more excitement from their electric scooter.

Regularly priced at $1,549, the Ausom F1 Max is available at the awesome price of just $1,429 for Electrek readers with code ElectrekFB.

Ausom isn’t done yet. They’re sweetening the deal for Electrek readers by throwing in a free gift with every scooter purchase. Buy any Ausom electric scooter between November 16th and 26th and you’ll get a free branded water bottle. From November 27th through December 1st, that gift switches to a branded water bottle carrier, giving late-season shoppers one more reason to take advantage of the best prices of the year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor sees new ways to put Bitcoin (BTC) to work on Wall Street.
  • According to staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bitcoin can be used to meet certain financial resource requirements for U.S.
  • It has been revealed that ‘Next step for adoption is using Bitcoin to work,’ Saylor wrote on X in response to the CFTC advisory published on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Strategy Executive Chairman Michael Saylor sees new ways to put Bitcoin (BTC) to work on Wall Street.

According to staff at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Bitcoin can be used to meet certain financial resource requirements for U.S. derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses.

It has been revealed that ‘Next step for adoption is using Bitcoin to work,’ Saylor wrote on X in response to the CFTC advisory published on Nov. 23.

As per the guidance, these companies must maintain sufficient financial resources to cover their operating costs for at least a year.

As clarified by CFTC staff, Bitcoin and Ether can be used to meet this requirement (as well as payment stablecoins). The advisory also provides guidance on how staff interpret the current rules. It also applies to swap execution facilities (SEFs), which are platforms where counterparties trade swaps.

Industry observers note that bitcoin holdings worth $10 million could count for $8 million toward the annual requirement, based on the minimum 20% discount that CFTC staff remarked they would accept. This provides some flexibility in case Bitcoin's price falls. The discount is also called a haircut.

Industry observers note that for Ether, the same minimum 20% haircut applies. For payment stablecoins, the haircut is 2%.

Industry observers note that this provides some incentive for an exchange to actually hold BTC. Exchanges could hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets and use some of its value to satisfy this reserve requirement. There would be no need to sell it for USD first.

Sources indicate that however, a futures exchange still needs to have sufficient unencumbered cash or highly liquid securities to cover its operating costs for at least six months. Bitcoin, Ether and even payment stablecoins do not fall into this category.

It has been revealed that the same six-month liquidity requirement applies to clearinghouses. Additionally, they need to maintain sufficient financial resources to cover a default by a clearing member.

CFTC staff also noted a potential downside for exchanges holding crypto reserves. During a market slump, there's a risk that an exchange's operating losses might rise. At the same time, the value of the Bitcoin it holds to cover those losses might fall.

So this possibility should be considered before an exchange decides whether to use Bitcoin to meet its financial resource requirements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

No doubt, tokenized equities have become one of the fastest-growing segments of the RWA market in 2026.

Binance Research reveals that the entire sector’s market cap increased to $3 billion. That’s a rise of in excess of 4x since the start of the year. Against this backdrop, Solana’s momentum in tokenized equities stands out.

As AMBCrypto reported, Solana has seen its tokenized equities weekly spot trading volumes reach an all-time high of $1.8 billion. This represents 43% of all on-chain equities, marking the highest proportion since June. Furthermore, tokenized stocks issued by Backpack Securities generated $1.39 billion in trading volume on Solana last week, marking their biggest week yet.

In essence, Solana [SOL] is directly benefiting from the growing interest in tokenized equities.

As an example, during the first 24 hours of listing, Anthropic’s tokenized stock raised $134.7 million on Solana, some 2.6x higher than the debut trading volume recorded by tokenized SpaceX shares. Furthermore, it attracted over 15,000 investors, underlining the growing interest in investing in both public and blue-chip listed businesses via blockchain. However, this momentum could extend beyond spot trading.

According to on-chain data, tokenized assets have become one of the fastest-growing DeFi categories in 2026. The key question is therefore whether Solana will be able to leverage its growing tokenized equity momentum to further develop its DeFi network and capture a larger share of this emerging market.

One of the biggest opportunities for tokenized assets lies in DeFi.

According to recent reports, the logic is simple: Investors can use these assets as collateral. This could help them back loans and allow borrowing too, hence increasing the practical application of tokenized assets. And while tokenized equities on DeFi have seen an impressive increase in value, rising by almost 1,800% within just one year ($14.9 million to $274 million), their overall adoption remains relatively low.

According to Token Terminal, the tokenized assets market is valued at $49.6 billion, but just $4.1 billion (8.2%) is presently utilized on DeFi platforms. This means that a large proportion of $45.5 billion is unused, highlighting the gap between tokenized asset growth and actual DeFi adoption.

Notably, this is where Solana’s growing tokenized equity activity becomes key.

Sources indicate that according to on-chain data, Solana has a 32% stake in total tokenized equity TVL valued at $87 million. Ethereum is next at 20%. Thus, Solana is well placed to continue to attract investment into tokenized assets. The next step is to build on this momentum by bringing more of these assets into DeFi through lending, borrowing and collateral markets.

With this in mind, Solana has the potential to enhance liquidity within its network. It can also enable tokenized assets to be used as collateral. It can then seek to claim more of the $45.5 billion of ‘missed’ DeFi value. This, in turn, makes Solana’s tokenized stocks momentum key to underpinning its DeFi position.

Solana’s tokenized equity activity is growing, with its market share reaching 32%.

Only 8.2% of tokenized assets are used in DeFi, leaving Solana room to attract more capital.

#122546. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data highlights a speed problem

Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data highlights a speed problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

In a recent development, the first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

Industry observers note that those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

The second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

Sources indicate that two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Recent findings suggest that across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider stated they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Recent findings suggest that those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

Recent findings suggest that the Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

In the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

Engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

Sources indicate that the Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

In a recent development, the Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

It has been revealed that what the data indicates is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

Industry observers note that to be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data demonstrates at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

According to recent reports, but it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

Perps and Swaps: How to Trade the News on Decrypt

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that readers have traditionally learned about markets in one place and traded them in another.
  • Decrypt set out to close that gap in September 2026, when it confirmed The Information Exchange: a network that brings together news, data, market prices, probabilities and the ability to trade, around the subjects readers follow.
  • The Information Exchange sees Decrypt delivering both the reporting and the market infrastructure that links information to trading, while the Solana blockchain provides the network on which trades settle, including token swaps and perpetual futures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that readers have traditionally learned about markets in one place and traded them in another. A story about Bitcoin, a public company or a commodity might shape a view, but acting on it meant opening an exchange or a trading app and starting over.

Decrypt set out to close that gap in September 2026, when it confirmed The Information Exchange: a network that brings together news, data, market prices, probabilities and the ability to trade, around the subjects readers follow.

The Information Exchange sees Decrypt delivering both the reporting and the market infrastructure that links information to trading, while the Solana blockchain provides the network on which trades settle, including token swaps and perpetual futures.

This guide explains what each one is and how to trade it on Decrypt.

Everything on The Information Exchange runs through a Decrypt Money Account, which released on Solana in October 2026.

Recent findings suggest that A Money Account holds one balance that funds every product on Decrypt: swaps, perpetual futures and prediction markets.The account is self-custodial, meaning Decrypt does not hold customers' private keys and cannot act on their behalf. It is designed to work without seed phrases, and network fees are covered, so users don't need to hold SOL, Solana's native token, to pay for transactions.

It has been revealed that in November 2026, Decrypt added confidential transfers, using Solana Privacy Rings from infrastructure firm Helius. Users can send funds without the amounts appearing on Solana's public ledger, and can switch the feature on by selecting "Enable" on the Private Balance panel of the Portfolio page. As of November 2026, privacy applies to transfers only, not to swaps or prediction market positions.

Solana Privacy Rings use zero-knowledge proofs, which let people prove they own and can spend a balance without revealing how much it holds.

According to recent reports, A swap exchanges one token for another at the current market price. Instead of placing an order on an exchange and waiting for it to fill, the trader sends one token and receives another in a single transaction.

Recent findings suggest that swaps on Decrypt are powered by Jupiter, a Solana trading platform that offers swaps, lending, borrowing, perpetual futures and portfolio tools. Jupiter finds prices across Solana's trading venues, so owners don't need to choose where a trade is executed.

At time of publication, swaps cover a select group of major cryptocurrencies and Solana tokens, as well as tokenized stocks, commodities and other real-world assets.

As of November 2026, the Assets panel of the Portfolio page groups holdings into crypto, stocks, commodities and collectibles, and lists tokens including SOL, BTC, ETH, XRP and HYPE.

According to recent reports, perpetual futures, or perps, are contracts that let traders bet on whether an asset's price will rise or fall without owning the asset. Unlike traditional futures, they have no expiry date. A trader who expects the price to rise goes "long," and one who expects it to fall goes "short.".

Industry observers note that perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets a trader control a larger position than their deposit would otherwise allow. Leverage magnifies gains and losses alike, and if the market moves against a position far enough, it can be liquidated, or closed automatically, wiping out the trader's margin.

Perps on Decrypt are powered by Phoenix, a fully onchain perpetuals exchange on Solana developed by Ellipsis Labs—making Decrypt the first media platform to offer perps trading alongside its journalism.

Each account trading on the XRP Ledger's decentralized exchange moved an average of 4,328 XRP a day in the third quarter of 2026, up 437% from 805 XRP in the same quarter a year earlier, according to a report that XRP treasury organization Evernorth released on Tuesday.

According to Evernorth, the average swap on the XRP Ledger reached 35 XRP in the third quarter, up from 19 XRP in the second quarter and under 6 XRP a year earlier. "The growth came from bigger trades, not more of them," the company wrote in the report.

It has been revealed that at the same time, the number of accounts trading on the XRP Ledger's order book fell to 1,042 a day in the third quarter of 2026 from 2,027 a day in the third quarter of 2025. The number stood at 1,203 in the fourth quarter of 2025, 1,324 in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,125 in the second quarter, according to the report.

Order-book volume on the XRP Ledger rose to 4.51 million XRP a day in the third quarter from 1.63 million XRP a day a year earlier, Evernorth data shows.

In total, 5.16 million XRP a day was traded on the XRP Ledger's exchange in the third quarter, and the figure was up 96% year over year, according to Evernorth.

Measured in U.S. dollars, exchange volume on the XRP Ledger fell 15% year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the report.

Evernorth also compared the XRP Ledger with Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana, Base, Arbitrum, Avalanche and Polygon. Across these seven networks, exchange volume in dollars fell 42% over the same period, the report highlights.

XRP was trading at around $0.93 on Tuesday morning after reaching as high as $1.026 on Monday, according to CoinMarketCap.

The report also reveals that the average balance of Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin on the XRP Ledger reached $937 million in the third quarter of 2026, up from $539 million in the second quarter. By the end of the quarter, the RLUSD balance on the XRP Ledger stood at $1.15 billion, compared with $670 million at the end of the second quarter, and the number of RLUSD holders on the network rose to 67,449 from 45,620.

According to Evernorth, the XRP Ledger's average share of RLUSD reached 48.5% in the third quarter, up from 34% in the second quarter. Still, Ethereum finished the quarter with more RLUSD than the XRP Ledger. Evernorth noted that on Ethereum, RLUSD "can already be lent," and that on the XRP Ledger, "native lending is in validator voting.".

As of Nov. 20, the Lending Protocol amendment had 24 of 35 validator votes, according to XRPScan. The amendment needs 29 votes, held for 14 days, to activate.

In a recent development, evernorth completed its business combination with Armada Acquisition Corp. II on Oct. 9, and its shares began trading on Nasdaq under the ticker XRPN on Oct. 12. The company entered the public markets holding approximately 473 million XRP, according to its press release.

Evernorth announced the deal in October 2025, with investments from SBI, Ripple, Pantera Capital, Kraken and GSR.

Industry News: Strategy sells $176M in MSTR shares for STRC buybacks – What’s behind the shift?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ambcrypto

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Michael Saylor’s Strategy is making headlines, but there is something under the wraps that is raising eyebrows.
  • In its 23rd November Form 8-K filing, the Bitcoin [BTC] DAT revealed that the company is becoming more aggressive with its capital management strategy, particularly when it comes to its preferred stock, STRC.
  • In fact, between 16th and 22nd November, the company sold 1,925,676 shares of its Class A common stock (MSTR), generating $176.7 million in net proceeds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michael Saylor’s Strategy is making headlines, but there is something under the wraps that is raising eyebrows.

In its 23rd November Form 8-K filing, the Bitcoin [BTC] DAT revealed that the company is becoming more aggressive with its capital management strategy, particularly when it comes to its preferred stock, STRC.

In fact, between 16th and 22nd November, the company sold 1,925,676 shares of its Class A common stock (MSTR), generating $176.7 million in net proceeds.

But here’s a catch: instead of directing the entire amount towards Bitcoin purchases, Strategy used just $29.6 million to acquire 457 BTC while allocating the remaining proceeds towards repurchasing STRC shares.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the tech giant bought back 2,183,747 STRC shares for approximately $211.8 million during the same period, using $147 million from MSTR share sales and another $64.8 million from its USD cash balance. Naturally, this has raised an vital question: why is Strategy selling one security to buy back another?

So, the difference lies in the roles of MSTR and STRC. MSTR, as we all know now, is Strategy’s common stock, offering investors exposure to its Bitcoin holdings and business performance. STRC, meanwhile, is a variable-rate perpetual preferred stock with a $100 stated value that pays regular dividends.

Recent findings suggest that therefore, Strategy aims to keep STRC trading around 99-100. When it trades below this range, buybacks can help support its market price while reducing outstanding shares and future dividend obligations.

This also explains the firm’s expanded buyback capacity. On 23rd November, Strategy increased its Digital Credit Securities repurchase authorization from $3 billion to $4 billion, with approximately $1.12 billion remaining. At the same time, it continues to use its ATM program to raise capital by issuing MSTR shares.

Given such a change in plans, Strategy still continues to be the largest BTC holder, with a total of 851,305 BTC, acquired at an aggregate cost of $64.23 billion and an average purchase price of $75,446 per BTC.

All in all, the filing highlights that Strategy is balancing Bitcoin accumulation with preferred stock buybacks rather than directing all its capital towards BTC purchases.

According to recent reports, this comes as the MSTR stock was trading at $84.40 at press time up by 8.48% in the past 24 hours. Meanwhile, STRC was trading at $98.26 at press time up by 5.01% in the past trading day.

Lastly, AMBCrypto’s recent report also highlighted this shift, as its MSTR shares were facing mounting pressure from Bitcoin’s decline, losing over 40% in Q4 2026.

However, one thing is clear, and that is continued MSTR weakness could make fresh capital raises more difficult, threatening Strategy’s future Bitcoin accumulation plans.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fidelity Investments now supports three newly introduced cryptocurrencies on its retail crypto trading platform: Chainlink (LINK), Aave (AAVE) and Uniswap (UNI).

The firm expanded from five available cryptocurrencies to eight on Nov. 24. In just one day, Fidelity added the same number of digital assets that it had added in the four years since it first made Bitcoin and Ether available for customer trading.

Sources indicate that eligible U.S. customers can trade these three tokens on the Fidelity website and app. Some states may have limited access to Fidelity's services.

Industry observers note that fidelity's three latest listings include tokens that represent different areas of decentralized finance. Aave is a lending protocol where people can deposit crypto assets to earn interest or use them as collateral for loans. AAVE token holders can vote on changes to the protocol's lending markets and other aspects of its operation.

Uniswap is a decentralized trading platform where customers can trade different tokens using shared pools of assets provided by other users. UNI is the Uniswap governance token.

Chainlink provides the data that blockchain apps need to operate. For example, a lending protocol might use a Chainlink price feed to assess the value of collateral for a borrower's loan. Chainlink (LINK) tokens are used to pay for services provided on its network.

Fidelity Crypto started accepting customers from its waitlist in November 2022. At the time, the only two cryptocurrencies it offered were Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH). By March 2023, Fidelity was offering its service to more eligible U.S. investors, but these were still the only cryptocurrencies it allowed customers to trade.

It has been revealed that on July 17, 2024, Fidelity added Litecoin (LTC) to its list of cryptocurrencies, bringing the total to three. Over a year later, on Oct. 23, 2025, the firm introduced Solana (SOL). In addition to individual retail accounts, Solana became available for crypto IRAs, wealth managers and institutional clients.

Industry observers note that fidelity added its fifth cryptocurrency on Feb. 4, 2026, when it released Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD) as its first stablecoin available to retail and institutional investors. Eligible people can exchange or redeem each FIDD token for $1. Fidelity waives its usual crypto trading fee when users exchange FIDD for dollars.

Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system.
  • Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.
  • Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

It has been revealed that solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that in the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” remarked Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

Industry observers note that by combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

It has been revealed that the researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

It has been revealed that that’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning newly introduced fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

Good way to think about the whole system. So what exactly does Don not-Quixote have against windmills?

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

The U.S. Department of Justice filed a civil forfeiture action on Nov. 23 seeking to recover more than $1.1 billion in USDC allegedly stolen from Binance by North Korean hackers.

In a recent development, the assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government. The latest filing represents another step toward recovering funds following the Oct. 29 attack, which reportedly resulted in more than $6 billion in stolen cryptocurrency.

The DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

In a recent development, U.S. authorities remarked they had helped freeze, seize or return more than $2.9 billion in cryptocurrency since the theft. The case highlights the role of cooperation between law enforcement agencies and crypto companies in tracking and recovering stolen digital assets.

Sources indicate that strategy purchased another 457 BTC for approximately $29.6 million, according to a Nov. 23 report based on the firm's SEC filing.

The latest acquisition was made at an average price of $64,898 per Bitcoin, bringing Strategy's holdings to approximately 851,305 BTC. The tech giant has spent around $64.23 billion accumulating Bitcoin at an average purchase price of $75,446.

The firm's recent purchase comes as the leading cryptocurrency has been struggling to rebound from the heavy sell-off that recently dragged it to a two-plus-year low.

  • Automation is not necessarily a upcoming occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “pump” trade could be taken to new extremes. While some may still be able to use their influence to promote a token, causing others to pile in, it could now be left up to AI to scour socials/wallet activity for abnormal trading volume, assess momentum rankings, etc. and execute on these opportunities faster than those that may be slower to react.

All things considered, agents may exacerbate many of the existing issues with crypto, from short lived moves/reversals, to dangerous herding and even more pronounced drawdowns.

Automation is not necessarily a upcoming occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.

A February 2026 study from the Journal of Futures Markets found sub-second trading patterns in BTC/ETH perpetual/spot markets exhibiting behavior consistent with algo trading for liquidity, increasing volatility and trading costs with no significant impact on prices.

In August 2026, Binance rolled out Agent OS allowing builders to access exchange trading functionality and data via AI agents.

Recent findings suggest that coinbase Ventures released a comprehensive breakdown of the crypto agentic stack from data, to agent building tools, to execution/compliance in November. Instead of dictating each trade, users may be able to assign high-level goals (i.e. follow momentum, hedge position, etc.) for agents to implement 24/7.

Automation will likely accelerate across the crypto space. While macro events, ETF inflows/outflows, large holders, etc. will still have an impact on Bitcoin, it’s likely that many more aspects/trades will become automated.

Time will tell how pervasive agentic trading will become, but the era of a small group of traders/influencers/chat rooms able to move the needle via FOMO/hype seems poised to face stiff competition from AI that never sleeps.

AI is not necessarily intelligent. A 2026 study published in the journal Frontiers in Blockchain studied machine-learning strategies using crypto market data and found that many strategies became highly overfit and offered no viable edge for retail traders once realistic trading fees were taken into account.

Also, strategies that performed well on one cryptocurrency did not necessarily perform well on others. Faster processing speeds can’t make bad data good, can’t identify all false narratives and can’t insulate a strategy from sudden shifts in market regimes.

Are institutional investors still relevant? Can they protect themselves? Absolutely.

Sources indicate that institutions are (and will continue to be) an vital source of capital, liquidity and price discovery (particularly for Bitcoin). A 2026 study using BTC data from 2012–2025 found that as the market has matured, Bitcoin has seen increased trading volume, decreasing transaction costs and increasing market efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that wintermute reported that in the first half of 2026 institutional clients accounted for 72% of total spot trading volume on its OTC desk (note: this is Wintermute’s OTC desk and is not representative of the entire market). It’s also worth noting that many institutional investors do employ quantitative strategies and state-of-the-art execution technologies.

While larger investors may have access to better data, faster infrastructure, cross-venue surveillance capabilities and stricter risk management protocols (and can limit their exposure and monitor abnormal order flow), there’s only so much that institutional investors can do to protect themselves.

Sources indicate that institutional investors can’t control a 24/7 global market with liquidity spread across multiple venues and derivatives markets. They also can’t assume that all AIs are created equal/safe (as Binance’s launch of its own AI demonstrated prompt injection risks and limited visibility into external AIs’ trading logic/reasons for trading).

Finally, during times of stress, risk management/contingency protocols (used by many investors) could be a crowded exit for funds that employ similar strategies.

The future is not “AI replaces every trader.” It will likely see continued automation of certain aspects of trading (i.e. execution, short-term alpha hunting, etc.) and a continued shift in the value-add that humans bring to the table (i.e. capital allocation, risk management, original research, granting/trading bots permission to trade, etc.).

While AI/bots may continue to squeeze spreads in normal market conditions, they may exacerbate drawdowns/cascades during times of market stress as strategies compete with one another.

At the end of the day, Bitcoin will still be bought/sold, it’s just a question of who gets to make those decisions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the U.S Department of Justice (DOJ) has taken legal action to recover more than $1.1 billion in cryptos stolen from Binance on 29th October 2026. With this move, the government has now moved beyond simply freezing the stolen funds and is now seeking their legal forfeiture.

According to the DOJ, the stolen funds had already been placed under a restraining order, which was the reason why they were prevented from being transferred or accessed while authorities pursued recovery efforts.

Sources indicate that remarking on the same, Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor remarked,.

The Department of Justice has long prioritized victims and their rights, and the commencement of this forfeiture action so soon after the restraint of these same assets reflects our commitment to ensuring that victims remain at the forefront of our work.

Binance suffered a cryptocurrency theft worth more than $6.3 billion, which the U.S authorities linked to North Korean cyber hackers.

Following the attack, the hackers allegedly used sophisticated laundering techniques to move the stolen cryptocurrency across different wallets and potentially convert it.

However, the FBI, U.S Secret Service, and the IRS has worked alongside private-sector companies to track the transactions and identify wallets holding the stolen funds.

It has been revealed that as its stands, the U.S. government has frozen and seized nearly $3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies from multiple sources since the Binance theft. The latest $1.1 billion forfeiture action is part of this broader recovery effort and does not represent an additional $1.1 billion on top of the nearly $3 billion already recovered or restrained.

If this forfeiture is successful, the action could help return the recovered assets to their rightful owners.
